page.h1: HTS Chapter 21: Miscellaneous Edible Preparations — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: Exporting Food & Supplements: Schedule B, FDA Certificates (HTS Ch. 21) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: HS and Schedule B codes for supplements, protein powder and sauces; why food is EAR99; FDA’s Certificate to a Foreign Government and free Certificate of Free Sale.
keywords: schedule b number for dietary supplements

intro: Food preparations, sauces, soups and supplements almost never need a U.S. export licence: they are **EAR99**, and even Cuba and Iran have routes for food (License Exception AGR and an OFAC general license). What U.S. agencies provide is the paperwork buyers’ countries ask for: **FDA export certificates** (a Certificate to a Foreign Government for conventional foods, and a free **Certificate of Free Sale** for dietary supplements), **USDA AMS** dairy certificates for ice cream and milk-based preparations, and **USDA FSIS** certificates for soups made with meat or poultry. A food made to a foreign buyer’s specification can be exported even if it does not meet U.S. rules, under section 801(e)(1) of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Manufacturers of syrups, drink mixes and other sugar-containing products can also use USDA’s sugar re-export program.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Chapter 21 Schedule B numbers start with the HS heading: dietary supplements, protein powders, drink mixes, flavored syrups and non-dairy creamers are usually 2106 (2106.10 for protein concentrates and textured protein, 2106.90 for the rest); sauces and seasonings 2103 (soy sauce 2103.10, ketchup 2103.20, mustard 2103.30, hot sauce, dressings and mixed seasonings 2103.90); soups, broths and bouillon 2104; ice cream 2105; instant coffee 2101.11 and coffee mixes 2101.12; yeast 2102. Vitamin or mineral pills put up as medicines can fall in Chapter 30, and whey or whey-protein concentrates in 0404 or 3502.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Food preparations, sauces, soups and supplements are EAR99 (not on the Commerce Control List), so most destinations need no licence. Food for Cuba goes under License Exception AGR after notifying BIS (15 CFR 740.18).

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.
steps.chapterNote: Food is treated more leniently than other goods: OFAC’s Iran regulations authorize exports of agricultural commodities, including food, under a general license with conditions (31 CFR 560.530). Check the destination’s OFAC program before quoting.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: The usual over-$2,500-per-Schedule-B-number rule applies. Exports to Country Groups E:1 and E:2 (Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria) need EEI whatever the value (15 CFR 758.1(b)(1)).

rules.agency: Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Human Foods Program
rules.title: Export certificates on request: a Certificate to a Foreign Government for conventional foods that may be sold in the U.S. ($175 for the first certificate, $155 for a second for the same products and request, $100 for each later one); a Certificate of Exportability for foods that cannot be sold in the U.S. but meet section 801(e)(1) (same fees); and a Certificate of Free Sale, with no fee, for dietary supplements, medical foods and foods for special dietary use (choose “Dietary Supplement” for any product with a Supplement Facts label). Apply online. FDA certifies U.S. status only; meeting the importing country’s rules is the exporter’s job.

citations.label: FDA: Online applications for export certificates for food

rules.title: Foods made for a foreign buyer: a food that does not meet U.S. requirements is not treated as adulterated or misbranded if it meets the foreign purchaser’s specifications, does not conflict with the importing country’s laws, is labeled on the outside of the shipping package as intended for export, and is not sold or offered for sale in the U.S. (FD&C Act section 801(e)(1), 21 U.S.C. 381(e)(1)).

rules.agency: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service (AMS), Dairy Grading Branch
rules.title: Dairy export certificates: the EU, China and Chile accept dairy products only from plants on export lists, and USDA AMS certifies only listed firms. This reaches ice cream (2105) and dairy-based preparations such as whey-protein blends, creamers with milk and coffee or tea mixes with milk powder.

rules.agency: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS)
rules.title: Soups, broths and bouillon made with meat or poultry under FSIS inspection need an FSIS export certificate for each consignment (9 CFR 322.2), and must meet the destination’s requirements in the FSIS Export Library.

groups.label: Coffee, tea & maté extracts and preparations; chicory
groups.note: Instant coffee and tea extracts need only FDA paperwork; coffee or tea mixes with milk powder follow the USDA AMS dairy route for the EU, China and Chile.

groups.label: Yeasts, dead single-cell micro-organisms & baking powder
Soups, broths & homogenized composite food (baby food)
groups.note: Soups and broths without meat or poultry are FDA foods; those made with meat or poultry under FSIS inspection need FSIS export certificates.

groups.label: Food preparations n.e.s.i. (supplements, syrups, mixes)
groups.note: Dietary supplements get FDA’s free Certificate of Free Sale; whey-protein blends, creamers with milk and other dairy-based preparations follow the USDA AMS dairy route for the EU, China and Chile.

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

savings.title: Use the EU’s reduced-duty quota for U.S. food preparations
savings.saves: About three quarters of the EU duty: for example 3.2% instead of 12.8% on food preparations n.e.s. and protein concentrates, 1.9% instead of 7.7% on sauces, 2.9% instead of 11.5% on soups.
savings.appliesTo: U.S.-origin goods of Chapter 21 listed in quota 09.9016, up to 250,000 tonnes per 12-month period from July 1, 2026; ice cream can also use dairy quota 09.9003 at 0%.
savings.document: The EU importer claims the quota order number on the customs declaration with proof that the goods originate in the U.S.
savings.caveat: First come, first served across all Chapter 21 goods; once the quota is used up, the normal rate applies until the next quota year starts on July 1.

savings.title: Have your Chinese buyer apply for a tariff exclusion
savings.saves: China’s 2018–19 counter-tariff on the goods: 10% on food preparations, ketchup and mustard, 25% on sauces, soups, coffee extracts and ice cream.
savings.appliesTo: U.S.-origin goods imported into China by an importer granted an exclusion under China’s market-based exclusion process; exclusions are valid until December 31, 2026.
savings.document: The Chinese importer applies through the State Council Tariff Commission’s exclusion process.
savings.caveat: The extra 10% on all U.S. goods is not excludable, and no extension past December 31, 2026 has been announced.

citations.label: White House: U.S.–China deal fact sheet, Nov 2025

savings.title: Use the Sugar-Containing Products Re-export Program
savings.saves: Lets you use sugar entered outside the U.S. raw-sugar tariff-rate quota for the sugar in exported syrups, drink mixes and other sugar-containing products.
savings.appliesTo: Manufacturers licensed by USDA who receive refined sugar from a licensed refiner and export an equivalent quantity of sugar as an ingredient in sugar-containing products.
savings.document: A USDA license (7 CFR 1530.102, 1530.104), with a bond or letter of credit; the equivalent sugar must be exported within 18 months of the transfer (7 CFR 1530.105).
savings.caveat: Sugar content is credited on a dry-weight, 100-degree-polarity basis, and records of every transfer and export must be kept.

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
